items.title: The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
items.snippet: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. items.title: Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
items.snippet: Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity. Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections.

items.title: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world
items.snippet: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have set the stage for ants to conquer the planet, with a surprising boost from “jumping genes” hidden in their DNA. Scientists discovered that bursts of activity from these mobile genetic elements coincided with the rise of major ant groups and may have helped sharpen their extraordinary ability to communicate through smell.

items.title: MapInsights helps police trainees learn the territory
items.snippet: In early 2026, the University of Illinois Division of Public Safety was facing a challenge. It had 11 security guards it planned to convert to community service officers, which meant they would change from being based in one building to working a whole beat.

items.title: Climate health harms outpace action, prompting calls for global health emergency
items.snippet: The 2026 Report of The Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change finds that many of the health risks and harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement was introduced (2016–2025) than in the decade before it (2006–2015).

items.title: Decoding the loopy physics of hula hooping with high-tech earthquake sensors
items.snippet: Hula hooping may be literal child's play, but as it turns out, the physics behind the gym-class staple is so complicated that scientists have spent decades trying to understand how the hula hoop defies gravity.

items.title: We studied 1,584 data centers—and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
items.snippet: Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they're up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return.

To better understand the consequences of these developments, long-term and comprehensive data are essential. items.title: The way Earth's 'thermostat' works may have changed during Pangea era
items.snippet: Life arose on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago, and our planet has remained habitable ever since—not too hot, not too cold. These life-sustaining conditions are possible in part thanks to a built-in, carbon cycle–based climate "thermostat" that controls the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

items.title: Identical vesicles, different behaviors: Model reveals how spontaneous asymmetry gives rise to lifelike behavior
items.snippet: In nonreciprocal active matter, agents act differently on each other, seemingly in violation of Newton's third law. This principle can result in various active matter traits, such as self-propulsion, molecular regulation and collective motion.

items.title: Can your brain make you see ghosts? The science behind the Bloody Mary legend
items.snippet: It's Halloween night. Someone has dared you to turn off the lights and stand in front of the mirror. The rules are simple: Stare into your reflection and say her name three times.

items.title: A 'simple recipe' takes some of the guesswork out of mass spectrometry imaging
items.snippet: A small sample of human tissue can hold a remarkable amount of information. Researchers can use it to search for molecular clues associated with cancer, investigate the chemical landscape of the brain or determine where a drug travels after it enters the body. Mass spectrometry imaging, or MSI, helps answer those questions by mapping where different molecules are located within tissue.

items.title: Rubin Observatory reveals its first dwarf planet candidate in our solar system
items.snippet: Scientists may add a new dwarf planet to the official roster of our solar system. The distant, icy body, provisionally dubbed 2026 ED138, orbits our system beyond Pluto. It was spotted earlier this month by a scientist combing through data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
